en: Preface to the Tiantai Commentary on the Lotus Sutra, composed by the Śramaṇa Shenhui of Tiantai. The Preface states:
The ultimate truth is nameless, yet names flow beneath the four heavens; the True Vehicle is unmoving, yet it moves...

Transcending the three realms, the realization of the teaching is凝然 (nengran—stabilized and immutable) within phenomena; the *siddhānta* adapts to conditions to transform sentient beings, drawing them forth without deliberate effort—what greater merit could there be!
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was preached by the Benevolent Hero upon his appearance in the world as the cause and condition for the One Great Matter.
Yet, as medicinal trees differ, they yield diverse results when moistened;
as capacities and dispositions are not uniform, those who receive the teaching also vary accordingly.
In its provisional manifestation, it is the wheel of Dharma of the Four Truths at the Deer Park;
in its revelation of the ultimate reality, it is the Pure Land of the three transformations on Vulture Peak.

Its purport is profound and its phrasing subtle; the person is honored and the Way is sublime. It elucidates the remote origin of the *āyus-pramāṇa* (lifespan) and reconciles the proximate traces of Gayā.
The rain and wind strike and disperse, casting aside the traps and snares of former teachings;
opening, showing, awakening, and entering, one obtains the fish and the rabbit of our present school.
Countless bodhisattvas increase their path and diminish their births.
The śrāvakas of the thatched hermitage feel shame for their small attainment and rejoice in the Great Vehicle.
King Bhaiṣajyarāja burned his own arm as an offering, and Prabhūtaratna manifested his entire body to bear witness; its ultimate perfection and profound subtlety are beyond the reach of words.
There was the Great Master of Tiantai, whose Dharma name was Zhiyi. In the past, he personally heard this scripture before the Tathāgata;
though his rank was only at the fifth stage, his reputation resounded through two reigns, and he attained a profound understanding of the Buddha-vehicle without ever attending a lecture hall.

Possessing the power of dhāraṇī and inexhaustible eloquence, he constantly lectured on the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for the Emperor at the Dajidian Hall; the Emperor, the possessor of ten thousand chariots, knelt before him, while the hundred officials snapped their fingers in approval.

Furthermore, as for the *Guānxīn* (Contemplation of the Mind) commentary, it wondrously transcends existence and non-existence; it takes true nature as its guiding principle and relies upon auxiliary illumination to achieve thorough penetration.
In its exposition of names to signify the core doctrine, it differs from the ancient masters; its fivefold analysis of principles all serves to support the sacred teachings.

Since the Venerable Zhi (Jizang) propagated the Dharma for over thirty years, he produced only the *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*. During the Sui Dynasty, by imperial decree of Emperor Yang, he composed these profound texts (*xuánwén*); these were actually the private notes of Dharma Master Guanding, totaling twenty fascicles. It is indeed true that "were it not for Zhi, they would not have been refined. These words are most certainly accurate.

More than one hundred years after his passing, during the *wùzǐ* year of the Tiānbão era in the Táng dynasty, there was the Venerable Lǎng of Qīngtài Temple in Dōngyáng Prefecture. He was a long-lived elder of the Dharma-gate and a pair of eyes and feet for the cooling pond [of the Sangha]. Equally diligent in both precepts and meditation, he encompassed both the internal and external disciplines; having attained the precious vessel of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra and dwelling in the stone chamber of Śūramgama, he would often sigh silently during his lectures, saying:
"Observing its underlying meaning, it is profoundly in accord with the Buddha-vehicle; yet examining its textual flow, there are occasionally instances where the sequence is disordered."

In some cases, the text continues while the meaning is interrupted; in others, the text follows after the meaning that precedes it. Sometimes a chapter is introduced at the beginning of the prose section, while at other times its meaning is directly explained following it. In verses, one may first state the number [of items], or later list their names without following a fixed order.
"However, the intention of the Sage is difficult to fathom; one can only look up to it with faith.
Now, because the various disciples have repeatedly urged me, saying:
"Those of superior capacity are easily enlightened and do not lose their way when investigating the profound mysteries;"
"Those of middling and inferior capacity, in following the literal text, lose its essential meaning.
If you would further deign to arrange it according to this sequence, the benefit would be immense.
The Upādhyāya deliberated on this matter repeatedly; having no other recourse, he focused his mind upon the Great Master to seek his approval or disapproval.
It was only through the inspiration received in a dream that the system was finally established in its proper order.
This was done out of consideration for circumstances and sincerity, rather than out of a desire to arbitrarily seek out similarities or differences by making additions or subtractions therein.

I hope that future scholars will understand this fundamental intent; seeking out and grasping the upper garment while discarding the lower, they shall take up the gold and cast away the gravel, preaching the Dharma of reality rather than being people of falsehood.

If one assists in the widespread fanning of the profound Dharma wind and prepares the additions and deletions for the Crimson Hills (Danqiu), then the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses will perfectly accord with the seal of the treasury, and the provisional city and the precious abode will both become intimate bridges to the ford.
Relying on the earnestness of Maitreya and turning back the reticence of Mañjuśrī, they assisted the six *pādas* of the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna* and extolled the single word of the *Chunqiu*.

Shenxiong and others all synthesized the preceding texts to clarify the subtle principles; there were none who had not previously resolved their minds together under the Buddha Śūnyarāja, and all sixteen śrāmaṇeras served as his successive lecturers.

Like cataracts meeting the sun, or clearing a blemish to nurture a pearl, I truly feel ashamed before the brush of Yanmen; how could I possibly fathom the profundity of Longpin? Yet, may those seekers of the profound, by bathing in this stream of the Way, find their foundation therein.
